Electron beam cross-linking reduces sheet resistance of 20 nm CNT films by up to 4 times at dosages below 10,000 mC/cm².
Nanopatterning with AAO nanopore arrays increases optical transparency of CNT films by 34%.
Micropatterning with nickel mesh increases optical transparency by 26%.
Nanopatterned CNT films show a 30% increase in Seebeck coefficient compared to unpatterned films.
CNT/PNIPAM nanocomposites achieve EMI shielding efficiencies of 20–30 dB with film thickness of a few micrometers.
PNIPAM exhibits a phase transition at 32°C, losing about 90% of its mass due to dehydration.
CNT/PNIPAM composites show a 40% temperature decrease in thermal signature reduction tests compared to 34–36% for controls.
E-beam irradiation changes CNT film color, indicating chemical or physical modification.
Sheet resistance initially decreases with e-beam dosage, then increases at higher dosages due to possible CNT damage.
Reactive ion etching (RIE) used for nanopatterning may chemically modify or damage CNT films, increasing resistance.
Nanopatterning length scale is smaller than intrinsic electron mean free path but larger than intertube scattering lengths.
CNT films prepared by membrane filtration and cross-linked by projection e-beam system.
CNT/PNIPAM composites prepared by dropcasting mixed solutions with 1% sodium dodecyl sulfate.
UV/vis spectroscopy, SEM, atomic force microscopy, four-point probe, vector network analyzer, and IR thermal imaging were used for characterization.

The CNT films maintain optical transparency after e-beam cross-linking and nanopatterning.
The CNT/PNIPAM composite films are lightweight, chemically stable, and mechanically strong.
The EMI shielding efficiency correlates strongly with electrical conductivity and inversely with optical transparency.
The nanopatterning method is compatible with large-area film production.
The research suggests potential for replacing indium-tin oxide (ITO) in transparent electrode applications.
